\section[rabugento]{rabugento — grumpy}

\label{lesson:PT-C474-rabugento}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for unfriendly, then the Portuguese for to offend.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: rabugento}
\textbf{rabugento} — \textquotedblleft{}grumpy\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
De manhã, antes do café, sou rabugento.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{In the morning, before coffee, I am grumpy.}
\end{quote}

Informal. \emph{Ser rabugento} is a trait; \emph{estar rabugento} is a mood.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{rabugento} is built on \emph{rabugem} \textquotedblleft{}mange in dogs\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), which goes back to Latin \emph{rōbīgō} \textquotedblleft{}rust, blight\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short): a grumpy person is as touchy as a dog with mange.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{rabugento}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{rabugento}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{rabugento}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for unfriendly, then the Portuguese for to offend, then say \emph{rabugento} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does rabugento mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Grumpy\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[resmungão]{resmungão — grumbler; grumbling}

\label{lesson:PT-C474-resmungao}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to offend, then the Portuguese for grumpy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: resmungão}
\textbf{resmungão} — \textquotedblleft{}grumbler; grumbling\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O meu avô é um resmungão, mas tem bom coração.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My grandfather is a grumbler, but he has a good heart.}
\end{quote}

Built on \emph{resmungar} \textquotedblleft{}to grumble\textquotedblright{} with \emph{-ão}; a woman is \emph{resmungona}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{resmungão} is built on \emph{resmungar} \textquotedblleft{}to grumble\textquotedblright{} with \emph{-ão} (EtymDB); the origin of the verb itself is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to offend, then the Portuguese for grumpy, then say \emph{resmungão} again

\section[amuar]{amuar — to sulk}

\label{lesson:PT-C474-amuar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for grumpy, then the Portuguese for grumbler.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: amuar}
\textbf{amuar} — \textquotedblleft{}to sulk\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Quando perde um jogo, o miúdo amua e não fala com ninguém.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{When he loses a game, the kid sulks and does not talk to anyone.}
\end{quote}

A sulk is \emph{um amuo}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{amuar} is built with the prefix \emph{a-} (EtymDB), but the origin of the rest of the word is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[a birra]{a birra — tantrum}

\label{lesson:PT-C474-birra}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for grumbler, then the Portuguese for to sulk.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a birra}
\textbf{a birra} — \textquotedblleft{}tantrum\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O menino fez uma birra no supermercado.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The little boy threw a tantrum in the supermarket.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Fazer uma birra} — to throw a tantrum. In Brazil \emph{birra} can also mean stubbornness.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{birra} is traced in EtymDB to Spanish \emph{birria}, which goes back to Latin \emph{verrēs} \textquotedblleft{}a boar\textquotedblright{}; the link is not certain.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a birra}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a birra}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a birra}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for grumbler, then the Portuguese for to sulk, then say \emph{a birra} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[choramingar]{choramingar — to whine, to whimper}

\label{lesson:PT-C474-choramingar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to sulk, then the Portuguese for tantrum.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: choramingar}
\textbf{choramingar} — \textquotedblleft{}to whine, to whimper\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O cão choramingava à porta.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The dog was whimpering at the door.}
\end{quote}

Built on \emph{chorar} \textquotedblleft{}to cry\textquotedblright{}: a small, whining cry.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{choramingar} is built on \emph{chorar} \textquotedblleft{}to cry\textquotedblright{}, which is inherited from Latin \emph{plōrāre} \textquotedblleft{}to wail\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
